newsitem.title: UK: Negative chart outlook seen adding to dollar woes.
newsitem.headline: Negative chart outlook seen adding to dollar woes.

text.p: An increasingly gloomy chart outlook is pushing the dollar lower as jitters ahead of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting next week also gnaw away at its fortunes, analysts said on Thursday.

Uncertainty about the timetable for European monetary union, concern about Japanese capital flows in the new financial year starting next month, and slowly shifting expectations that German and Japanese interest rates might not stay low forever have also taken some of the shine off the dollar.

"Quite a lot of factors are turning against the dollar now," said Brian Kiely, treasury analyst at Royal Bank of Scotland in London. "It's generally looking weak, and the technical moves we've seen this morning, in particular against the Swiss franc, are not encouraging."

The dollar has eroded several important chart points this week. Against the mark, technical analysts are now eyeing the late February low at 1.6670 as the next major support, which if eroded would open the way for a sharper decline, possibly of about three pfennigs.
"Erosion of 1.6665/80 would confirm a more protracted downmove," said Francoise Skelley, head of global trading technical analysis at Credit Suisse First Boston.
Skelley said the key to the dollar's fortunes is its movements against the Swiss franc, which fell to its lowest level in over five weeks at 1.4325 in European morning trading today.
The dollar's speedy decline from three-year highs at 1.4922 Swiss francs in early March to today's low is seen as a warning signal.
Some analysts predict a slide to major psychological support at 1.40 Swiss francs, which would take the dollar back to its lowest level since January.

Against the yen, the dollar is also close to key support levels. "The dollar needs to hold 122.50/00 trendline and congestive support to prevent a slide to 120.90 and then the key 120.00 area," said Alan Dunne, technical analyst at Bank of America.

The dollar traded at 1.6785 marks and 122.55 yen during midafternoon trade in Europe, down from 1.6821 and 122.70 yen in late European trade on Wednesday. Against the Swiss franc, it was at 1.4385, down from 1.4445.
Yet, the approach of the U.S. central bank's Federal Open Markets Committee's (FOMC) meeting on Tuesday is likely to prevent a slide for now, analysts said.
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan signalled on Thursday that the U.S. central bank was inching toward raising interest rates, possibly next week.
In prepared testimony to Congress's Joint Economic Committee, Greenspan said the U.S. economy retained a "great deal of vigor" and the jobs market was strong.
"The risk for the dollar is on the downside, but it's not going to face a major sell-off ahead of the FOMC meeting," said Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago in London.

"Improving perceptions about German economic growth and the increased scepticism about EMU are not helping the dollar," said Knuthsen. Also weighing on the dollar is the current correction of overbought bond markets as investors are becoming more risk averse, which has helped to boost the mark at the expense of the lira, the Swedish crown and the peseta.
